analysis.one_liner: Shields employers from age-discrimination claims when they convert traditional pensions into cash balance accounts.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had no cosponsors, never received a vote and died in committee when the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change pension rules so employers could convert traditional pensions into cash balance account plans without violating the age discrimination rules in ERISA. To test whether an older worker loses out, plans could ignore the value of early-retirement subsidies, and the rules would apply to plan years before the bill passed. It was sent to two House committees and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers that sponsor traditional defined benefit pensions, especially those that have converted or want to convert them into cash balance account-style plans. The bill would give them a legal safe harbor against age-discrimination claims, let them disregard early-retirement subsidies when testing benefit reductions, apply the new rules retroactively to past plan years, and set rules that would legitimize cash balance account balances as satisfying pension vesting requirements.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Employers converting pensions to cash balance plans

how_it_helps.text: Gives employers a safe harbor from age-discrimination liability: a plan passes the test if an older worker's accrued benefit is at least as large as that of an otherwise identical younger worker, even if the plan cut the older worker's benefits.
Lets plans ignore the subsidized portion of early retirement benefits when making that comparison, removing the main source of age discrimination claims over cash balance conversions.

Provides that cash balance account-style plans satisfy pension vesting and nonforfeitability rules as long as the balance discounted at a market interest rate covers the promised benefit, giving plan sponsors legal certainty on a design that had drawn lawsuits.
Applies to plan years beginning before, on, or after enactment, so it would retroactively bless past conversions and changes that are currently being challenged.

analysis.who_pays: Older workers in pension plans that convert to cash balance accounts. Their early-retirement subsidies would be ignored when checking whether they lose benefits compared with younger coworkers, so benefit reductions that hit them hardest would no longer count as age discrimination, and their early-retirement options could be worth less.
analysis.who_pays_short: Older workers in converted pension plans

drawbacks.text: The comparison test disregards the subsidized portion of early retirement benefits, which are concentrated in the accrued benefits of older long-service workers, so plans could cut exactly those benefits without violating age discrimination law.
The rules would apply retroactively to plan years before enactment, cutting off pending challenges by workers whose benefits were already reduced by past conversions.

Recognizing account-balance accruals as satisfying minimum vesting rules would lock in cash balance plan designs that often freeze or wear away the benefit growth older workers had expected under a traditional pension formula.

The safe harbors for Social Security offsets and permitted benefit disparities would allow plan designs that treat older and younger workers differently, as long as the offset formula does not trigger at a specified age.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit is legal certainty for employers, and it is real: the ambiguity over whether cash balance conversions discriminate by age was producing lawsuits. But the certainty is purchased by narrowing the protections of older workers, the very people the age discrimination rules were written for. Disregarding early-retirement subsidies in the comparison means the plan only has to match a younger worker's base benefit, not the richer package older workers actually earned, and the retroactive effective date would erase claims already in dispute. On balance, the costs to older workers' retirement security outweigh the employer-side benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to two House committees and then a subcommittee, and never got a vote before the 109th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Boehner introduced the bill on June 9, 2005, and it was referred to the Education and the Workforce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee.
On July 25, 2005, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations, and no further action was taken.
The bill had no cosponsors and never received a vote in the House or Senate before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

The bill's core provision would let a plan pass the age discrimination test if an older worker's accrued benefit equals that of an otherwise identical younger worker, while disregarding the subsidized portion of early retirement benefits in that comparison.
The new rules would apply to plan years beginning before, on, or after enactment, reaching past pension conversions.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Older workers in traditional pension plans, whose protections against benefit cuts tied to age stayed in place because the bill never advanced. Employers with cash balance conversions gained nothing, since the legal uncertainty they wanted resolved was not resolved by this bill.

for.name: Rep. John Boehner
for.role: House sponsor; Chairman, House Education and the Workforce Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill; it was referred to two committees and then to a subcommittee, where it stayed until the Congress ended.

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without a markup or floor vote for the remainder of the 109th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were taken and no other member of either party signed on; the bill had a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors.

industries.industry: Large employers with defined benefit pension plans
industries.note: The bill gives these employers a legal safe harbor to convert traditional pensions into cash balance accounts without facing age discrimination claims, and it would apply retroactively to past conversions. The cost of that certainty falls on older workers whose early-retirement subsidies and benefit accruals would be reduced with legal protection.
